title: Decompensated heart failure: increased sympathetic nervous system activity
vignette: A 63-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to dyspnea. Over the past several days, the patient has experienced progressively worsening shortness of breath while walking his dog around the block. In addition, he could not breathe while lying in bed last night and fell asleep only after moving to a recliner. The patient had an acute myocardial infarction 2 years ago and has been nonadherent with his medications and follow-up appointments. Temperature is 36.7 C (98 F), blood pressure is 122/74 mm Hg, pulse is 94/min, and respirations are 22/min. Physical examination shows bibasilar lung crackles, jugular venous distension, and bilateral pitting edema in the lower extremities. Chest x-ray reveals cardiomegaly and pulmonary venous congestion. Which of the following factors is most likely contributing to this patient's symptoms?

clues.note: Progressive exertional dyspnea reflects worsening pump function and pulmonary congestion in heart failure.

clues.text: could not breathe while lying in bed last night
clues.note: Orthopnea (dyspnea when supine, relieved by sitting up in a recliner) indicates volume overload/pulmonary congestion in decompensated heart failure.

clues.text: acute myocardial infarction 2 years ago and has been nonadherent
clues.note: A prior MI (ischemic cardiomyopathy) plus medication nonadherence sets up decompensated heart failure - the low cardiac output triggers maladaptive neurohormonal activation.

clues.text: bibasilar lung crackles, jugular venous distension, and bilateral pitting edema
clues.note: Crackles + JVD + peripheral edema confirm biventricular congestive heart failure with volume overload.

whatMatters: Decompensated heart failure (prior MI, orthopnea, JVD, edema, congestion) lowers cardiac output, triggering compensatory neurohormonal activation. The main maladaptive driver perpetuating symptoms is INCREASED SYMPATHETIC NERVOUS SYSTEM ACTIVITY (plus RAAS), causing vasoconstriction (increased afterload) and fluid retention. Answer E.
strategy: In heart failure, reduced cardiac output activates the SYMPATHETIC nervous system and RAAS. These raise afterload and preload, worsening the failing heart (a vicious cycle) - so 'increased sympathetic activity' (E) is contributing. Trap: BNP is also increased (choice D), but BNP is a beneficial/compensatory response (vasodilation, natriuresis) that's overwhelmed - it doesn't 'contribute' to the deterioration. Reject the 'decreased' options (A, B, C), which are the opposite of what occurs.

options.text: Increased plasma brain natriuretic peptide concentration

eliminations.label: Decreased arteriolar resistance - reversed
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: lower systemic vascular resistance would reduce afterload. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: in heart failure, sympathetic/RAAS activation INCREASES arteriolar resistance (vasoconstriction), not decreases it. ✅ Correct if: a vasodilated/distributive state.

eliminations.label: Decreased plasma renin activity - reversed
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: low renin would reduce RAAS activity. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: reduced renal perfusion INCREASES renin/RAAS activity in heart failure. ✅ Correct if: a low-renin state (e.g., primary hyperaldosteronism).

eliminations.label: Decreased ventricular end-diastolic pressure - reversed, your pick
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: lower filling pressure would reduce congestion. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: in decompensated HF, end-diastolic (filling) pressures are INCREASED from volume overload and impaired emptying - that's why there's pulmonary congestion. ✅ Correct if: a hypovolemic/underfilled state.

eliminations.label: Increased BNP - a beneficial/compensatory response
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: brain natriuretic peptide IS elevated in HF and is a useful marker. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: BNP promotes vasodilation and natriuresis (helpful) - it opposes, rather than 'contributes to,' the symptoms, and its beneficial effects are overwhelmed by sympathetic/RAAS activation. The trap is that it's elevated, but the question asks what CONTRIBUTES to the symptoms. ✅ Correct if: asking which marker is elevated/used diagnostically.

reasoning: Prior MI + orthopnea + JVD + edema + congestion = decompensated (congestive) heart failure
Reduced cardiac output triggers compensatory neurohormonal activation
Sympathetic activation and RAAS raise afterload and retain fluid, perpetuating the failure
-> increased sympathetic nervous system activity contributes; answer E
mechanism: Decompensated heart failure begins with reduced cardiac output and elevated filling pressures. The initial drop in blood pressure/perfusion triggers compensatory neurohormonal activation - chiefly the SYMPATHETIC nervous system and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). Sympathetic activation increases heart rate and contractility and causes arterial/venous vasoconstriction (raising afterload), while RAAS activation retains sodium and water (raising preload). These responses transiently support perfusion but, over time, increase cardiac workload and drive deleterious remodeling, perpetuating a downward spiral of worsening congestion and symptoms - so increased sympathetic activity is a key contributor. In this setting, arteriolar resistance, renin activity, and ventricular end-diastolic (filling) pressures are all INCREASED (the 'decreased' options are reversed). Brain natriuretic peptide is elevated too, but it is a counter-regulatory hormone (promoting vasodilation and natriuresis) whose beneficial effects are overwhelmed - it opposes, rather than contributes to, the symptoms.

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid CV > heart failure neurohormonal activation: sympathetic + RAAS increase afterload/preload and cause remodeling; natriuretic peptides are counter-regulatory.

difficulty.label: 🧭 Understanding the question
difficulty.message: Distinguish a DELETERIOUS contributor (sympathetic activation) from a beneficial-but-overwhelmed response (BNP), and note that the 'decreased' options are reversed.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on afterload/preload, end-diastolic pressure, RAAS, renin, or BNP? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: BNP (D) is elevated but is compensatory/beneficial - not a contributor. Options A/B/C are the wrong direction (all are increased in HF). Your pick (C) is reversed.

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: HF -> low output -> sympathetic + RAAS activation (up afterload/preload) -> vicious cycle; BNP is counter-regulatory (beneficial but overwhelmed).

memoryHook: A failing pump panics: sympathetic + RAAS clamp the vessels and hoard fluid - helping for a moment, harming for good. BNP tries to help but gets outnumbered.
